anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to process or retain far more data and rows than business logic requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or subscribers fall behind because they cannot receive or apply primary-generated log records at the production rate.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated physical or logical storage for data, logs, or temporary areas reaches exhaustion, impeding normal allocation and recycling.

When all three exist concurrently, the system exhibits extreme and widening replica lag, growing on-disk log backlogs, and escalating disk-space consumption on both primary and replicas. Long-running or chatty transactions produced by inefficient SQL inflate the volume of redo, generate oversized result sets that spill to temp space, and keep locks open longer. Replicas struggling to apply these bloated change batches accumulate ever larger relay or archive logs; the primary cannot purge its own logs, and free space plummets. Users observe increasing statement latency, frequent timeouts, stalled or cancelled writes when log destinations fill, stale read-only traffic on replicas, and emergency auto-extend or out-of-space errors in data, temp, or log areas.

Causally, sub-optimal workload logic produces excessive data modifications and prolonged transactions, which directly amplifies the replication stream. The overwhelmed replication path slows, causing unapplied logs to pile up. Because those retained logs occupy the same filesystems or object stores as data, they accelerate space consumption and can eventually exhaust capacity. Imminent space exhaustion further degrades replica apply throughput (due to I/O contention and pause-on-error behavior) and can halt primary DML when log writes or temp allocations fail. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others in a feedback loop: inefficient SQL inflates log volume, replication delay prevents log recycling, accumulated logs and temporary spill exceed storage limits, and storage pressure in turn magnifies both latency and replication backlog, culminating in a compound performance and availability crisis.

entry.official_description: Using ASSIGN_GTIDS_TO_ANONYMOUS_TRANSACTIONS creates limitations on the replication topology - you cannot fail over between downstream and upstream servers. Only use this option if it is not possible to enable GTIDs on the source, for instance, because of lack of permissions. If possible, use the procedure for enabling GTID transactions online instead, as described in the documentation.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with log shipping, replica apply state, replication-channel configuration, or cross-node communication needed to keep replicated state consistent.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect replication channel health, sender/receiver state, log retention, downstream apply lag, and network stability between replication endpoints.
